title: Maximum Product of a Non-Decreasing Triplet
statement:
You are given an array `A` of `n` positive integers. Choose three indices `i < j < k` such that `A[i] ≤ A[j] ≤ A[k]` (the three values, read from left to right, never decrease) and the product `A[i] * A[j] * A[k]` is as large as possible.

Print the maximum possible product. If no three indices satisfy the condition, print `-1`.

Equal values are allowed, and the same value may appear in all three positions as long as the indices are different.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
The second line contains `n` space-separated integers `A[0] ... A[n-1]`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the maximum product, or `-1` if there is no valid triplet.

examples.explanation: Picking the values 3, 4, 6 at indices 2, 3, 5 gives 3 * 4 * 6 = 72. Using the 5 at index 1 would give at most 2 * 5 * 6 = 60 because only 2 lies to its left and is not larger than it.
The array is strictly decreasing, so no pair of indices i < j has A[i] ≤ A[j].
Three of the four 4s form the triplet 4, 4, 4 with product 64. The 2 cannot help: it has nothing smaller before it.

hints: Fix the middle index j. For a fixed j the best triplet uses the largest allowed value on the left and the largest allowed value on the right, because every value is positive.
On the right, the largest value in the suffix after j is the best choice, provided it is at least A[j]. Precompute suffix maxima.

On the left you need the largest earlier value that is at most A[j]. Maintain a Fenwick tree (or a sorted structure) indexed by value that answers prefix-maximum queries as you sweep j from left to right.
